response: {"title":"Boundary-first counterexample check","intervention":"Before running broad regression tests, spend at most one quarter of the remaining verification time constructing and executing one minimal counterexample for each changed cross-module contract, then use the remaining time for the narrowest existing regression tests covering those contracts.","claim":"Relative to no appended instruction, this bounded boundary-first instruction will improve hidden-test pass_rate without increasing deadline misses on fixed-deadline multi-module Python tasks.","mechanism":"Minimal counterexamples directly exercise assumptions at module seams where locally correct edits often compose incorrectly, producing fast, actionable failures before more expensive regression runs.","assumptions":["Changed cross-module contracts can be identified from signatures, call sites, or data flow.","A useful minimal counterexample can usually be created within the quarter-time cap.","The environment permits focused test or script execution."],"risks":["Counterexample construction may duplicate existing coverage.","Subtle stateful or concurrency failures may not admit a minimal quick check.","The one-quarter cap can crowd out regression tests on short deadlines.","Incorrectly inferred contracts can generate irrelevant failures."],"test_plan":{"experiment":"Assign matched multi-module Python tasks randomly to the instruction or no-instruction control under identical model, tool, and deadline settings; score final patches with hidden tests and record whether each run completes before deadline.","metrics":["pass_rate","wall_time","turns"],"success_condition":"The treatment has higher pass_rate and a deadline-miss rate no greater than control, with wall_time and turns used to characterize the verification cost."},"single_shot_ordinal":3}
